warmup.q: A limiter runs n = INCR rl:card:7, then if n == 1: EXPIRE rl:card:7 60, and refuses attempts once n passes 5. A pod is OOM-killed right after its INCR returned 1. What happens to card 7?
options: Nothing: Redis expires the key after 60 seconds anyway
The key never gets a TTL, so after a few more attempts card 7 is refused for good
The next INCR returns 2 and sets the missing EXPIRE
Redis undoes the INCR because the connection closed
warmup.why: Only the attempt that saw 1 sets the TTL, and that pod died. Every later attempt sees 2, 3, 4 and skips the EXPIRE, so TTL rl:card:7 stays -1 and the counter never resets. Redis has nothing to undo: the INCR was a complete command, and the EXPIRE was never sent.

sections.h: A rate limit is a shared counter with a deadline
sections.html:
Card testing looks like this in the logs: one stolen card number, 300 authorization attempts in a minute, each with a different CVV, until one is approved. The fraud rule that stops it is simple: at most 5 attempts per card per minute. The question is where the count lives.

The simplest version keeps a counter per card in each pod's memory. It breaks as soon as you run 20 pods behind a load balancer: each pod allows 5, so the card gets 100 attempts a minute. The count has to be shared, and lesson 1 already gave you the tool. INCR rl:card:7 adds one on the server and returns the new value, and because one thread runs each command to completion, 20 pods calling it at once never lose an increment.

The count must also start over every minute. That is a fixed window: the minute is the window, and the counter resets when it ends. Let the first attempt of the window start a 60-second TTL (lesson 4's per-key deadline), and the key deletes itself:

Java
long n = redis.incr("rl:card:7");
if (n == 1) redis.expire("rl:card:7", 60);     // the first attempt of the window starts the clock
boolean allowed = n <= 5;
Kotlin
val n = redis.incr("rl:card:7")
if (n == 1L) redis.expire("rl:card:7", 60)     // the first attempt of the window starts the clock
val allowed = n <= 5

This works until a pod dies between the two commands. The pod is OOM-killed, or its connection drops, right after the INCR that returned 1. Now rl:card:7 holds 1 and has no TTL. The next attempt gets 2, so it doesn't set the TTL either, and neither does any attempt after it. The counter never resets, and from the sixth attempt on, card 7 is refused for good. The Redis docs describe this race on the INCR page. It is lesson 6's model again: one command runs alone, a sequence doesn't, and a sequence can also stop halfway.

The fix is to make it one command. A Lua script can run INCR and EXPIRE together (the Try it below has it). Redis 8.8 added a built-in for exactly this: INCREX rl:card:7 BYINT 1 UBOUND 5 EX 60 ENX adds one unless that would pass 5, and sets a 60-second TTL in the same command. ENX means "only if the key has no TTL yet". Without it, every admitted attempt restarts the 60 seconds and the window stretches. The reply is two numbers, the new value and the amount actually added, so [5, 0] means "refused".

That is the model for this lesson. For every request, each pod asks Redis one question, "may this go ahead?", and Redis must answer and record the answer in one command, with a deadline on the record so that it cleans itself up. The rest of the lesson changes what the record holds: a log of times, a bucket of tokens, and finally a payment's stored response.

sections.h: A sliding window remembers when each attempt happened
sections.html:
A fixed window has a seam at every minute boundary. Five attempts at 0:59.0 to 0:59.4 fill minute 0. Five more at 1:00.0 to 1:00.4 fill minute 1, which started empty. The limit said 5 a minute, and the card got 10 in 1.4 seconds. The demo below measures exactly that.

What the rule means is "at most 5 in any 60 seconds, counted back from now". That is a sliding window. To count it you need to know when each recent attempt happened, not just how many there were, so the record becomes a log: one entry per admitted attempt, with its time.

Lesson 2's sorted set fits. Each member is one attempt with a unique id, and its score is the time in milliseconds. Members stay ordered by score, so dropping the old ones is one range command. For an attempt at time now:

  1. ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rl:card:7 -inf <now - 60000> drops every attempt that is 60 seconds old or older.
  2. ZCARD rl:card:7 counts what is left.
  3. Fewer than 5: ZADD rl:card:7 <now> <id> and PEXPIRE rl:card:7 60000, then admit. Otherwise refuse and record nothing. If you recorded refusals, a card that kept trying would never get back under the limit.

Sent as separate commands from the pod, this breaks the way lesson 6's balance did. Two pods both run ZCARD, both read 4, both ZADD: 6 attempts admitted. In the demo, 32 threads each sent one attempt at the same instant, and the separate-commands version admitted 9 in one run and 10 in another. Not 32, because Jedis's pool has 8 connections, so only about 8 threads sit between their ZCARD and their ZADD at a time. The same steps in one Lua script admitted exactly 5, every time. The lab's SlidingWindowLimiter is that script.

Two details matter. The member must be unique. Use the timestamp as the member and two attempts in the same millisecond become one member, so the second is never counted; use a UUID. And someone has to say what time it is. The lab passes the pod's clock in, so the tests can control it. Pods synced by NTP differ by a few milliseconds, which doesn't matter for a 60-second window. If it does matter, call redis.call('TIME') inside the script, and every pod uses Redis's clock.

The price is memory: one member per admitted attempt. A limit of 5 per minute costs 5 members per card. A limit of 10,000 per hour per merchant costs 10,000 members, while the next section's bucket needs two numbers whatever the limit.

steps: With the server running, run WindowDemo (Java) or WindowDemoKt (Kotlin) from the labs folder. The demo passes made-up times to the limiters, so the boundary falls at the same place on every run.

sections.h: A token bucket allows a burst, then a steady rate
sections.html:
Some clients are bursty by design. A merchant's refund job sends 40 requests in one second at the end of every hour and nothing in between. A limit of 5 per minute refuses most of that burst. A limit of 40 per second lets a broken client send 40 every second, forever. What you want is "a burst of up to 10, then 2 per second on average".

That is a token bucket. Picture a bucket that holds at most 10 tokens and gains one every 500 ms. Each request takes a token, or is refused if the bucket is empty. A client that was quiet finds a full bucket and can spend all 10 at once. After that it gets one request per new token: 2 a second.

You don't need a timer that adds tokens. Store two numbers per client: tokens, how many were left after its last request, and ts, when the bucket was last refilled. On each request, work out how many tokens were earned since ts, add them (never above 10), then take one. In Redis the two numbers live in a hash, and the read, the arithmetic and the write are one script, for the same reason as before: two pods must never both take the last token.

The worked example below builds it. Two choices in it matter. It counts whole tokens: the script adds floor(elapsed / 500) tokens and moves ts forward by exactly that many intervals, so the part of a token not yet earned isn't lost, and no floating-point error builds up. And its TTL is the time to refill from empty: after 5 quiet seconds the bucket would be full anyway, so Redis may delete the key, and the next request starts with a full bucket.

In the demo, a burst of 15 at t = 0 got 10 through. Then one request every 250 ms got every other one through, 10 of 20, which is 2 per second. After 5 quiet seconds another burst got 10 again.

Which one should you use? A fixed window with INCREX is one key and one command, and its seam lets up to twice the limit through. That is fine for coarse abuse limits such as 1,000 requests per minute per IP. The sliding log is exact and costs a member per request: use it for small limits where exactness matters, such as card velocity rules. The token bucket costs two fields per client and is the usual shape for API quotas. If you'd rather not write Lua, Redisson's RRateLimiter keeps a rate limiter in Redis for you (trySetRate(RateType.OVERALL, 2, Duration.ofSeconds(1)), then tryAcquire()).

code.html: package sfz.redis.l07.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import java.util.List; /** A token bucket in Lua: 10 tokens, one new token every 500 ms. A burst of 15, then one request every 250 ms. */ public class TokenBucketDemo { // KEYS[1] the bucket (a hash with tokens and ts). ARGV[1] capacity, ARGV[2] ms per new token, ARGV[3] now in ms. static final String TOKEN_BUCKET = """ local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1]) local interval = tonumber(ARGV[2]) local now = tonumber(ARGV[3]) local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts') local tokens, ts = tonumber(b[1]), tonumber(b[2]) if tokens == nil then -- a bucket nobody used yet starts full tokens, ts = capacity, now end local earned = math.floor((now - ts) / interval) -- whole tokens since ts if earned > 0 then tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + earned) ts = ts + earned * interval -- keep the part of a token not earned yet end local allowed = 0 if tokens > 0 then tokens = tokens - 1 allowed = 1 end redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ts) redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], capacity * interval) -- idle that long, it is full again: forget it return allowed """; static final String KEY = "demo:l07:bucket:merchant:m-17"; static boolean take(RedisClient redis, long now) { Object r = redis.eval(TOKEN_BUCKET, List.of(KEY), List.of("10", "500", String.valueOf(now))); return Long.valueOf(1).equals(r); } public static void main(String[] args) { try (RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { redis.del(KEY); long t0 = 1_762_500_000_000L; // a pretend clock, passed in, so every run is the same int burst = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) if (take(redis, t0)) burst++; System.out.printf("t = 0.00 s a burst of 15: %2d admitted, %d refused%n", burst, 15 - burst); StringBuilder line = new StringBuilder(); int steady = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) { boolean ok = take(redis, t0 + i * 250L); if (ok) steady++; line.append(ok ? sections.h: An idempotency key turns a retry into a replay
sections.html:
The card issuer answered in 120 ms. The checkout service's HTTP client had a 100 ms timeout, so it gave up and sent the payment again, and your service charged the card a second time. Nothing was broken. Retries are how clients survive a network that drops packets, and a client that times out can't tell whether its request was lost or only the response was.

So the server has to recognize a retry. The client makes up one key per payment, usually a UUID, and sends it with every attempt in an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the response of the first attempt under that key, and answers every retry with the stored response instead of doing the work again. Stripe's API works this way: it saves the status code and body of the first request and keeps keys for at least 24 hours. The IETF has a draft standard for the header, at version 08. To the client, a retry looks like the first answer arriving late.

The simplest version is lesson 5's cache-aside: GET idem:k-7f3a, return the stored response on a hit, otherwise charge and SET the response. It breaks when two copies of the same request are in flight at once, and that is exactly the timeout case: the retry arrives while the first attempt is still waiting for the issuer. Both GETs miss, both pods charge. Check-then-act, again.

So claim the key before doing the work, in one command. SET idem:k-7f3a <pending> NX PX 30000 succeeds for exactly one request, and every other request finds the key taken. Add GET, and the same command also tells the loser what is there: SET key value NX GET (the two options are allowed together since Redis 7.0) returns nil when it stored your value, and the existing value, untouched, when it didn't. One round trip, and no gap between "is it there?" and "it's mine".

The value says what state the payment is in. While the first attempt works, it is PENDING. When the charge returns, the pod replaces it with DONE plus the exact response body, with a TTL of 24 hours. A retry that finds PENDING gets 409 Conflict, meaning "try again shortly". A retry that finds DONE gets the stored response, byte for byte. The stepper plays the timeout case from start to finish.

try.title: Claim a key, collide with a retry, replay the answer
steps: At a redis-cli prompt (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), run the DEL, which clears an earlier run, and the first two SETs. The second one plays the retry: same key, same body hash, a new attempt token.
Finish the first attempt with the XX SET (write only if the key exists), then send a third attempt. Predict its reply.
Read the TTL. How long will this key answer retries?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
DEL idem:k-7f3a
SET idem:k-7f3a P|h-4f1c|t-1 NX GET PX 30000
SET idem:k-7f3a P|h-4f1c|t-2 NX GET PX 30000
PTTL idem:k-7f3a
SET idem:k-7f3a 'D|h-4f1c|{"payment":"p-981","status":"approved"}' XX PX 86400000
SET idem:k-7f3a P|h-4f1c|t-3 NX GET PX 30000
TTL idem:k-7f3a

try.expect: The first DEL prints (integer) 0, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. The first SET prints (nil): the key was free, and attempt t-1 owns it now. The second prints "P|h-4f1c|t-1": NX refused, and GET showed a PENDING with the same hash, so this retry should get 409. PTTL is just under 30000. The XX SET prints OK. The third attempt prints "D|h-4f1c|{\"payment\":\"p-981\",\"status\":\"approved\"}" (redis-cli escapes the inner quotes): DONE with the same hash, so the server sends that body back. TTL prints (integer) 86400: retries are answered for a day.

refs.title: SET: NX, GET and the IFEQ conditions

sections.h: The record must say what it was for, whose it is and when to give up
sections.html:
Three things go wrong with a record that only says PENDING or DONE, and each one adds a part to it.

The first is a key reused for a different request. A client bug sends a 40-euro payment with the key of yesterday's 12.50-euro payment. The store finds DONE and replays "approved, 12.50". The client believes the 40 euros were paid, and nothing was charged. So the record stores a hash of the request body, a fingerprint, and a request whose hash differs gets 422 Unprocessable Content. The IETF draft asks for these status codes: 409 while the first request is still being processed, 422 for a key reused with a different body.

The second is a pod that dies while its record says PENDING. Every retry then gets 409, forever. So PENDING gets its own short TTL, longer than the slowest attempt can take. With a 10-second issuer timeout, 30 seconds is enough. After that a retry can claim the key again.

That TTL creates the third problem. Attempt 1 is slow, and its PENDING expires. The retry, attempt 2, claims the key and starts. Then attempt 1 comes back from the issuer with a decline and writes DONE over attempt 2's record. Attempt 2 is approved and writes its DONE too, or it finishes first and attempt 1 overwrites it. Either way the stored answer may not match what happened last. So PENDING carries a random token for its attempt, P|<hash>|<token>, and finishing is a compare-and-set: write DONE only if the key still holds exactly my PENDING. On Redis 8.4, SET key <done> IFEQ <my pending> PX 86400000 does it in one command; before 8.4 it is a three-line Lua script. A stale attempt's write changes nothing. The lab's IdempotencyStore is this record.

One gap is left, and Redis can't close it alone. If a pod charges the card and dies before writing DONE, its PENDING expires, and the next retry charges again. Close that gap where the money moves. Send the same idempotency key to your payment provider if its API accepts one, as Stripe's does, or write the record in the same Oracle transaction as the payment row. Redis is the fast front: it stops the duplicates that arrive while the first attempt is running, and every one after it finished.

try.title: Refuse a stale attempt and a reused key
steps: Clear the key, then claim k-9c01 as attempt t-1. Then DEL it again, which plays the 30-second PENDING TTL running out while attempt 1 is stuck at the issuer.
Let the retry, t-2, claim the key. Now play attempt 1 coming back late with a decline, then attempt 2 finishing with an approval. Predict both replies.
Finally send the same key with a different body hash, h-9b20.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt (lines starting with # are notes)
code.html:
DEL idem:k-9c01
SET idem:k-9c01 P|h-4f1c|t-1 NX GET PX 30000
# 30 s pass: attempt t-1's PENDING expires
DEL idem:k-9c01
SET idem:k-9c01 P|h-4f1c|t-2 NX GET PX 30000
SET idem:k-9c01 'D|h-4f1c|{"status":"declined"}' IFEQ P|h-4f1c|t-1 PX 86400000
SET idem:k-9c01 'D|h-4f1c|{"status":"approved"}' IFEQ P|h-4f1c|t-2 PX 86400000
SET idem:k-9c01 P|h-9b20|t-3 NX GET PX 30000

try.expect: The first DEL prints (integer) 0, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. Both claims print (nil), and the second DEL prints (integer) 1. Attempt 1's late SET ... IFEQ P|h-4f1c|t-1 prints (nil): the key holds t-2's PENDING, so the stale decline is refused. Attempt 2's prints OK. The last SET prints "D|h-4f1c|{\"status\":\"approved\"}". The stored hash is h-4f1c and this request's is h-9b20, so the server answers 422 and must not replay the approval.

refs.title: The Idempotency-Key HTTP header field (IETF draft)

analogy: Go back to lesson 1's bank branch with its one fast teller. For rate limits she keeps a tally sheet per card, with "throw away at 10:01" written at the top. The sliding window is a sheet where she writes down the time of each visit and crosses out visits older than a minute. The token bucket is a jar of 10 tokens on her desk that an assistant tops up at a fixed pace. For idempotency, every withdrawal slip carries a number the customer chose. Before paying out, she pins a note to the board, "slip 7f3a: being handled", and when she's done she files a carbon copy of the receipt under that number. A customer who comes back with the same slip gets a copy of the receipt, not a second payout. The analogy breaks on memory: a teller would recognize a returning customer after a week, while Redis forgets the slip number the moment its TTL ends, and a retry after that is a brand-new payment.
world: Your payment services retry all the time without anyone writing a retry loop. Temporal retries an activity that timed out. A Kafka consumer redelivers a batch after a rebalance. A Quarkus REST client annotated with @Retry retries on a timeout. Each of these needs an idempotency key that stays the same across retries: the payment id or the workflow id plus the activity id, never a fresh UUID per attempt. The Redis record catches the concurrent and later duplicates cheaply, and the same key passed to the payment provider or a unique constraint in the Oracle payments table catches the crash-after-charge case. Rate limits show up in the same services: a velocity rule on attempts per card (a sliding log, small and exact), a quota per merchant API key (a token bucket), and a cap on calls to an issuer that allows 200 TPS from your whole fleet (a shared bucket every pod draws from).
mistake: The most common mistake is the idempotency check written as GET, then do the work, then SET the response. It passes every test that sends one request at a time, and fails in production exactly when it matters: a client times out at 100 ms and retries while the first attempt still waits for a 120 ms issuer, both GETs miss, and the card is charged twice. People write it that way because it is cache-aside, which is right for caching and wrong for claiming. Claim the key first with one command, SET key PENDING NX GET PX 30000, do the work only if you got nil, and finish with a compare-and-set to DONE. The same shape of bug sits in rate limiters written as INCR followed by a separate EXPIRE.

compare.title: An idempotent charge handler in Java and Kotlin

java.title: ChargeHandler.java
java.html: record Reply(int status, String body) {} // POST /payments: the Idempotency-Key header and the raw JSON body Reply charge(String idemKey, String requestJson) { String hash = sha256(requestJson); // same body, same hash IdempotencyStore.Begin begin = store.begin(idemKey, hash); if (begin instanceof IdempotencyStore.Begin.Replay replay) return new Reply(200, replay.getResponse()); if (begin instanceof IdempotencyStore.Begin.InProgress) return new Reply(409, "{\"error\":\"in progress\"}"); if (begin instanceof IdempotencyStore.Begin.Mismatch) return new Reply(422, "{\"error\":\"key reused\"}"); IdempotencyStore.Begin.Started started = (IdempotencyStore.Begin.Started) begin; String response = issuer.authorize(requestJson); // the side effect, once per key store.complete(idemKey, hash, started.getToken(), response); return new Reply(200, response); }

kotlin.title: ChargeHandler.kt
kotlin.html: data class Reply(val status: Int, val body: String) // POST /payments: the Idempotency-Key header and the raw JSON body fun charge(idemKey: String, requestJson: String): Reply { val hash = sha256(requestJson) // same body, same hash return when (val begin = store.begin(idemKey, hash)) { is Begin.Replay -> Reply(200, begin.response) Begin.InProgress -> Reply(409, """{"error":"in progress"}""") Begin.Mismatch -> Reply(422, """{"error":"key reused"}""") is Begin.Started -> { val response = issuer.authorize(requestJson) // the side effect, once per key store.complete(idemKey, hash, begin.token, response) Reply(200, response) } } }

compare.note: Both handlers call the lab's Kotlin IdempotencyStore and send the same Redis commands: one SET ... NX GET before the charge and one SET ... IFEQ after it. The difference is how the four outcomes are handled. Kotlin's when over the sealed Begin interface is checked by the compiler: add a fifth outcome and this function stops compiling until you handle it. Java sees the Kotlin data objects as classes with a single instance, so it tests them with instanceof, and nothing warns you when a case is missing. A Java version of the store would declare Begin as a sealed interface of records and use a pattern-matching switch to get the same check. Neither handler stores the reply's status code; a real one would keep it next to the body so a replay of a 4xx also returns the same status.

worked.title: A token bucket in one Lua script

steps.say: Start with the state. A bucket is a hash with two fields: tokens, what was left after the last request, and ts, when the bucket was last refilled, in milliseconds. HMGET reads both in one call, and missing fields come back as false, which tonumber turns into nil. A bucket nobody has used yet starts full.
steps.code:
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local interval = tonumber(ARGV[2])     -- ms per new token: 500 means 2 per second
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens, ts = tonumber(b[1]), tonumber(b[2])
if tokens == nil then                  -- a new bucket starts full
    tokens, ts = capacity, now
end

steps.say: Refill without a timer. Count the whole tokens earned since ts, add them up to the capacity, and move ts forward by exactly those intervals. The leftover part of an interval stays in ts for the next request, so 250 ms plus 250 ms still earns a token, and integer arithmetic never drifts.
steps.code:
local earned = math.floor((now - ts) / interval)
if earned > 0 then
    tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + earned)
    ts = ts + earned * interval
end

steps.say: Take one token or refuse, write both fields back, and set the TTL to the time a bucket takes to refill from empty. A bucket idle that long is full again, so forgetting it changes no answer.
steps.code:
local allowed = 0
if tokens > 0 then
    tokens = tokens - 1
    allowed = 1
end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ts)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], capacity * interval)
return allowed

steps.say: Call it with the bucket's key and three arguments. The script's 1 or 0 arrives as a Long. This is the demo's call: 10 tokens, one every 500 ms, and the caller's clock.
steps.code: boolean take(String merchant, long nowMillis) { Object r = redis.eval(TOKEN_BUCKET, List.of("bucket:" + merchant), List.of("10", "500", String.valueOf(nowMillis))); return Long.valueOf(1).equals(r); }

alt.html: fun take(merchant: String, nowMillis: Long): Boolean = redis.eval(TOKEN_BUCKET, listOf("bucket:$merchant"), listOf("10", "500", nowMillis.toString())) == 1L

steps.say: Pick the clock last. Passing now in makes the script testable and its output repeatable, and NTP keeps pods within milliseconds of each other. If pods' clocks can't be trusted, read Redis's own clock inside the script instead: local t = redis.call('TIME') returns seconds and microseconds, so now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000). Since Redis 7.0 a script may read TIME and still write, because replicas receive its writes rather than re-running it (lesson 6).

drill.title: The fixed-window limiter from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write allow(card) for 5 attempts per card per 60 seconds as one Lua script called with Jedis: INCR, set the TTL only on the first attempt, return the count. Then name the Redis 8.8 command that replaces the script, with its options.

answer.html: static final String FIXED_WINDOW = """ local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]) if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end return n """; boolean allow(String card) { long n = (Long) redis.eval(FIXED_WINDOW, List.of("rl:" + card), List.of("60")); // one command: never TTL-less return n <= 5; } // Redis 8.8: INCREX rl:<card> BYINT 1 UBOUND 5 EX 60 ENX; allowed when the applied increment (2nd reply) is 1

alt.html: val FIXED_WINDOW = """ local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]) if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end return n """.trimIndent() fun allow(card: String): Boolean { val n = redis.eval(FIXED_WINDOW, listOf("rl:$card"), listOf("60")) as Long // one command: never TTL-less return n <= 5 } // Redis 8.8: INCREX rl:<card> BYINT 1 UBOUND 5 EX 60 ENX; allowed when the applied increment (2nd reply) is 1

recap: A limiter's check and its record must be one command. INCR and EXPIRE as two calls can leave a counter with no TTL that never resets.
Fix the fixed window with a Lua script or Redis 8.8's INCREX ... EX 60 ENX. Even then, up to twice the limit gets through across a boundary.
A sliding-window log is a sorted set of timestamps that one script trims, counts and adds to: exact, at one member per admitted request.
A token bucket stores two numbers per client and allows a burst up to its capacity, then a steady rate.
An idempotency key is claimed with SET ... NX GET before the work. PENDING carries the body hash, an owner token and a short TTL; DONE carries the exact response for 24 hours.
A pod that charges and dies before DONE still needs the payment provider's idempotency or the database transaction to stop a second charge.

explain.prompt: A teammate proposes: GET idem:<key>, charge the card if it's missing, then SET idem:<key> <response> EX 86400. Explain what goes wrong and what the record needs instead.
explain.answer: Two copies of the same payment are often in flight at once: the client times out after 100 ms and retries while the first attempt still waits for the issuer. Both GETs miss and both pods charge. The check and the claim have to be one command, so the record is written before the charge: SET key PENDING NX GET PX 30000 stores it for exactly one request and tells every other request what is there. Then the record needs more than a state. A hash of the body, so a key reused for another payment gets 422 instead of somebody else's response. A short TTL on PENDING, so a crashed pod doesn't block the key forever. And a random owner token in it, so a slow attempt that comes back after its PENDING expired can't overwrite the new owner's record; finishing is SET ... IFEQ <my pending>. DONE holds the exact response for 24 hours, and retries get it back byte for byte. A pod that charges and dies before DONE still leaves a gap, which the provider's idempotency key or the database transaction has to close.

deeper.html:
The sliding window counter. When a log per subject is too big, approximate it with two fixed-window counters: this minute's count, plus last minute's count weighted by how much of last minute still overlaps the 60 seconds before now. Fifteen seconds into a minute, 45 of last minute's 60 seconds are still inside, so the estimate is current + 0.75 × previous. It costs two small keys whatever the limit, and it assumes last minute's requests were spread evenly. It can be wrong by a few requests either way, which is fine for an API quota and not for a fraud rule.

Where the limiter runs. A limit kept in Redis costs one round trip per request, about 0.2 ms on the lab laptop (lesson 1). If a limit only protects your own service from overload, a limiter inside each pod, such as Resilience4j's, set to the total divided by the number of pods, needs no network at all; it drifts when the pod count changes. Limits that are business rules, such as attempts per card, need the shared count.

Choosing the idempotency key. The key must be the same on every retry of one logical operation, and different for different operations. For an HTTP client, a UUID created once per payment and kept across retries. For a Kafka consumer, the payment id or the record's topic, partition and offset. For a Temporal activity, the workflow id plus the activity id. A fresh UUID per attempt is the classic mistake: every retry looks new.

Storing the status code. The lab stores only the response body. A real record also keeps the HTTP status and any headers the client depends on, so that a replay of a 402 or 422 is the same answer as the original.

Redis Cluster. Every script here touches one key, so limiter and idempotency keys spread across Cluster slots without hash tags (lesson 11).
